summary: This informational document describes a URN namespace identifier for resources published by the Defence Geospatial Information Working Group, managed through its registry system.

plainLanguage.summary: This registers a name style for map-data resources so they have stable names.

questions: what is the dgiwg urn namespace
how does dgiwg name geospatial resources
subtitle: A namespace identifier for defence geospatial resources and specifications.

tldr.problem: The Defence Geospatial Information Working Group (DGIWG) creates standards and specifications for sharing geospatial information across military and defence organizations. These resources need unique, persistent identifiers to avoid conflicts and ensure reliable references.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6288 registers a URN Namespace Identifier (NID) called 'dgiwg' that allows DGIWG to assign URNs with the structure urn:dgiwg:{resource-type}:{resource-specific-string}, managed by the DGIWG Registry System (DRS).
tldr.outcome: The 'dgiwg' namespace is now an official IANA-registered URN namespace, enabling DGIWG to uniquely identify resources such as coordinate reference systems and feature-attribute data across military applications.

today: RFC 6288 is an Informational RFC that registered the 'dgiwg' URN namespace with IANA in 2011. The namespace remains active and is used by DGIWG to manage geospatial resources and standards.

sections.title: The DGIWG and Its Need for Identifiers
sections.content:
The Defence Geospatial Information Working Group is a multinational organization serving the defence ministries and military organizations of member nations. It develops standards and practices for creating, exchanging and using geospatial information—maps, coordinates, feature descriptions and spatial data—essential for NATO operations and allied peacekeeping missions.

DGIWG standards are built on ISO standards for geographic information and incorporate service specifications from the Open Geospatial Consortium. As DGIWG defines more data models and encoding formats, it needs unique, permanent names for these resources so that when an application references a resource, everyone interprets it the same way.

For reliable XML namespaces in their specifications, DGIWG decided to register a formal URN namespace with IANA rather than embed references in multiple documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The DGIWG is a team of military organisations that work together on how to share map information. They need official names for all their different kinds of information so everyone knows what they mean.

sections.title: The DGIWG URN Structure
sections.content:
The registered namespace identifier is dgiwg. All URNs in this namespace follow a two-part structure after the NID:

urn:dgiwg:{DGIWGresource}:{ResourceSpecificString}

The DGIWGresource part is a case-sensitive label for a class of resources—such as crs for coordinate reference systems or fad for feature-attribute data. Each resource class has its own naming rules covered in DGIWG standards documents.

The ResourceSpecificString is the unique identifier within that resource class. For example, a coordinate reference system for WGS 84 might be urn:dgiwg:crs:WGS84, and a specific geographic feature might be urn:dgiwg:fad:dfdd:Aerodrome:aerodrome.
sections.plainLanguage: Each DGIWG name has two parts: what kind of thing it is (like 'map coordinates' or 'building type') and its specific name. That way you always know what you are looking at.

sections.title: Registry and Management
sections.content:
The DGIWG Registry System (DRS), managed by DGIWG, is the authority responsible for assigning resource types and maintaining registries. It publishes lists of registered resources and procedures for requesting new ones, similar to how IANA manages Internet registries.

URNs assigned by the DRS are permanent and cannot be reassigned. DGIWG maintains separate sub-registries for each resource type; for example, a CRS registry and a Feature-Attribute-Data registry. The DRS also permits experimental URN values for testing, though these are not registered permanently.

DGIWG coordinates with other standards bodies—ISO and the Open Geospatial Consortium—to avoid naming conflicts and to ensure consistent use of terms across standards organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: DGIWG keeps an official list of all the names they have given out and makes sure no two things get the same name. They also work with other groups so everyone uses the same names.

sections.title: Real-World Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows two concrete examples of how DGIWG URNs are used. The first is a coordinate reference system:

urn:dgiwg:crs:myname
This references a specific coordinate system defined in DGIWG's CRS registry, which can be looked up to get the precise latitude-longitude transformation parameters.

The second example uses the Feature-Attribute-Data resource class:

urn:dgiwg:fad:dfdd:Aerodrome:aerodrome
This identifies a specific feature type (aerodrome) in the Feature-Attribute-Data registry, with standard codes and names for military geographic features like helipads and movement-area lighting.

These URNs allow military mapping systems to reference features and coordinate systems in an unambiguous way across all alliance members.
sections.plainLanguage: One URN might say 'use this particular way to measure coordinates on Earth.' Another says 'this is the name for an airport.' When two countries' systems talk to each other, they use these official names so they agree about what everything is.
